extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, platform designers, and scholars of scholarly communication interested in peer review innovation
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts standards, criteria, and desiderata for assessing or designing peer review processes and platforms for research manuscripts, including technical, social, ethical, and evaluative dimensions. Focuses on pre- and post-publication review models, transparency/anonymity options, incentives, and evidence-based evaluation of innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criteria: quality, novelty, validity, and potential impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is the process in which experts are invited to assess the quality, novelty, validity, and potential impact of research by others, typically while it is in the form of a manuscript for an article, conference, or book (Spier, 2002).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four dimensions are presented as the core evaluative targets for reviewers and underlie many variants of peer review; they determine suitability for journal placement, contribution to knowledge, and are central to traditional peer review's function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: The criteria used for evaluation, including methodological soundness or expected impact are important variables to consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many modern venues vet submissions based on the soundness of the research rather than perceived impact (e.g., PLOS, PeerJ). Methodological rigor includes appropriate design, analysis, and reproducibility considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected impact (or importance) is a key evaluative criterion used by reviewers and editors to judge manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact judgments influence selection and gatekeeping; the paper notes peer review often fails to recognize the most impactful research and cautions reliance on impact as sole criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of the review process (open vs closed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review comes in various flavors that result from different approaches to the relative timing of the review and the transparency of the process (what is known to whom about submissions, authors, reviewers and reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency affects traceability of revisions, accountability of reviewers, and the degree to which the community can interrogate decisions; the article contrasts open review with opaque traditional systems and highlights trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of review (pre-publication vs post-publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different approaches arise from relative timing of the review (with respect to article drafting, submission, or publication); models include publish-first-filter-later and post-publication review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish-first models (e.g., arXiv, F1000Research) decouple dissemination from vetting, increasing speed and visibility but require moderation/filters and new incentive structures for quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity models: single blind, double blind, open
rubrics_metrics.description: Over time, three principal forms of journal peer review have evolved: single blind, double blind, and open. Single blind: reviewers anonymous, authors known; double blind: both anonymous; open: identities transparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each model has operational costs and benefits: single blind is common due to lower cost; double blind is effortful to anonymize; open promotes accountability but may affect candor and create perceptions of retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control as a core trait
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the traits underlying a viable peer review system is quality control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality control can be achieved via gatekeeping, soundness checks, methodological review and editorial oversight; different systems implement quality control differently (pre-publication vetting vs post-publication moderation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantified performance metrics as engagement incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantified performance metrics as engagement incentives is a trait underlying viable peer review systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes platforms may use metrics/reputation systems to incentivize reviewers and participants (e.g., Publons, platform-level metrics), but warns about perverse incentives and the need to design metrics carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Certification and reputation are traits underlying a viable peer review system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review serves to certify research quality and confer reputational signals; any new system must deliver credible certification or reputation mechanisms that the research community accepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias reduction and fairness (including language equity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Efforts to reduce systemic bias and issues such as linguistic inequality for non-native English authors are important evaluative concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper links bias reduction to Mertonian norms (disinterestedness) and highlights that peer review can perpetuate biases (e.g., suppressing radical ideas, disadvantaging non-native English speakers). Systems should be evaluated on their propensity to reduce such biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to detect fraud and serious errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review's effectiveness in detecting fraudulent or incorrect work is a crucial evaluative dimension; studies show it can fail to detect fraud and gross defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A robust peer review system should be evaluated on sensitivity to fraud and major errors; the article cites evidence that traditional review is often poor at detecting fraud, motivating alternative checks (e.g., data review, statistical review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and data peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Data peer review and the verification of reproducibility are important components of modern peer review evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note data peer review is a vast topic; good practice includes availability of data, evaluation of datasets, and review processes that assess reproducibility of analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise and competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer selection should ensure reviewers are knowledgeable and competent to assess the manuscript's content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper (and reviewers' comments) emphasize variability in reviewer proficiency and the lack of formal training; reviewer competence is a key quality dimension and may require training or accreditation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and incentives for reviewers (credit, payment, discounts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals sometimes reward reviewers with free subscriptions, APC discounts, or payment; platforms like Publons enable claiming recognition for review activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition systems should be designed to properly attribute reviewer contributions (via ORCID, Publons) and to align incentives without creating perverse effects; the article discusses both paid and voluntary recognition models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor role and decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors mediate reviewer reports and ultimately make publication decisions; the relation between editors and reviewers is central to the system's functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems should be evaluated on transparency of editorial decisions, editorial accountability, and how editor-reviewer tensions are managed; interactive public peer review shows editors still decide even when public comments are solicited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization and metadata for peer review activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardizing peer review activities (descriptions, metadata) enables attribution, recognition, and potential reward for peer review labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article suggests standardizing how peer review is described (not the activity itself) to facilitate recognition; linked identifiers (ORCID, CrossRef) help describe and attribute review work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence base and experimental evaluation of peer review innovations
rubrics_metrics.description: New peer review systems and innovations require evidence and experimental evaluation to demonstrate effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers urge stronger emphasis on rigorous evaluation (randomized trials where possible) and the development of core outcome sets and measurement standards for peer review research (PEERE, Peer Review Congress).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost, time, and efficiency (including redundancy and reviewer fatigue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review consumes significant time and money; issues include publication delays, reviewer fatigue, and redundant reviewing across venues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective systems should minimize unnecessary delay and redundant effort (e.g., reuse of reviews across journals), and consider the economic cost of peer review alongside time burdens on reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community engagement and critical mass
rubrics_metrics.description: Success for new peer review platforms relies on reaching a critical threshold of research community engagement with both the process and the platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs must incentivize community participation; without sufficient engagement, reputation and certification mechanisms fail and platform benefits aren't realized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceability and auditability of review-to-revision processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Open traceability of the discussions and revisions that led to final publication is an evaluative desideratum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closed systems make it impossible to trace substantial revisions; transparent review or published referee reports enable auditing of how articles changed and why decisions were made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation thresholds and filtering for non-scientific content
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-print servers and publish-first platforms often apply moderation to filter out non-scientific content rather than full peer review (e.g., arXiv moderation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms should define moderation criteria (non-scientific content thresholds) and be transparent about what moderation does/does not guarantee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish-first / filter-later (decentralized dissemination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoupling dissemination from peer review via publish-first, filter-later protocols (e.g., arXiv) changes the function and evaluation of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These models prioritize rapid dissemination and rely on community moderation, commenting, or overlay journals for certification; they require complementary mechanisms for quality signaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical infrastructure and community-led platforms (OJS, overlay journals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical platforms (e.g., Open Journal Systems) and overlay journals provide infrastructure to manage peer review and restore community control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infrastructure choices affect cost, scalability, editorial workflows, and accessibility; OJS examples show low-cost, community-driven options that enabled many journals to operate, especially in developing regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage peer review and Registered Reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-stage peer review and Registered Reports (pre-results acceptance of methods) are models designed to reduce bias and evaluate methods prospectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These approaches aim to reduce publication bias and reward sound methods; the paper suggests integrating clinical trial registration history where appropriate and highlights Registered Reports as an innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication commenting and annotation platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms for post-publication commenting (e.g., PubPeer, PaperHive) allow ongoing community review and critique after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-publication systems broaden scrutiny but require moderation, incentivization, and reputation mechanisms; they may complement or replace traditional pre-publication gatekeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactive Public Peer Review (discussion papers with public commentary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactive Public Peer Review posts manuscripts as discussion papers; reviewer reports are posted alongside the manuscript and the community is invited to comment prior to formal publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model (used by Copernicus journals and others) combines invited referee reports and spontaneous community comments; editors still decide on acceptance and may request revisions after discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training and minimum competency standards
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little formal training for peer reviewers; establishing training programs and minimum standards (e.g., Publons Academy) is proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer training could improve review quality and consistency; the paper and reviewers recommend integrating training and possibly credentialing into peer review ecosystems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core outcome sets and measurement approaches for peer review research
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little agreement on how to measure peer review; the development of core outcome sets is needed to standardize measurement across studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without standardized outcomes, aggregation and systematic review of peer review interventions is difficult; the paper cites Bruce and others on optimal designs and measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical oversight and publication ethics (COPE guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: COPE (Committee on Publication Ethics) provides guidelines addressing abuse and misconduct during the publication process; ethical oversight is an evaluative standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems should adhere to publication ethics standards, have procedures to handle misconduct, and ensure ethical clarity in reviewer/editor/author interactions; the paper notes COPE's guidance on peer review came later in its history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language equity and accessibility for non-native English authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can lead to linguistic inequality and language-oriented research segregation for non-native English speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider whether systems disproportionately disadvantage non-native English authors and what remedies (language support, inclusive policies) are in place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of persistent identifiers and cross-platform recognition (ORCID, CrossRef, CC licenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifiers and licensing (ORCID, CrossRef, Creative Commons) can mediate recognition, attribution, and discoverability in community-mediated overlay journals and review systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrating identity and metadata standards supports attribution of review labor and linking review activity to researcher profiles; the paper queries how such services mediate quality control and recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against reviewer retaliation and safeguarding early-career authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns exist about retaliation against reviewers or negative consequences for authors when reviews are negative; safeguarding mechanisms are an evaluative requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper discusses perceptions of retaliation (and limited documented evidence) and stresses the social dimension: ensuring strong, honest, constructive feedback is received without abuse, and mechanisms exist to address misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid platform design combining social web traits
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed novel hybrid platform model should combine traits of social Web platforms (transparency, reputation, engagement) to resolve technical and social issues in peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design evaluation should consider how platform features (e.g., reputation systems, commenting, metrics) interact with scholarly incentives and whether they avoid replicating existing biases or creating perverse incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of status-quo protection and openness to radical/innovative research
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should avoid protecting the status quo and suppressing research viewed as radical, innovative, or contrary to referees' perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems should be assessed on whether they enable or hinder novel research; closed opaque processes may disproportionately suppress radical ideas—designs that increase diversity and openness may mitigate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of reviewer workload and strategies to reduce redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer fatigue and redundancy from multiple rounds of review across journals are recognized problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should include how systems reduce redundant reviewing (sharing reviews across journals, transfer options), limit reviewer burden, and streamline workflows to maintain reviewer willingness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus versus editor-driven decisions in public review models
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactive public peer review may include public comments but acceptance decisions are still taken by editors rather than relying on consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs should clarify decision rules (editor judgment vs consensus) and be transparent about how public input influences final outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity options and their implications for constructive feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing reviewers to be anonymous or named has implications for honesty, constructiveness, and perceptions of retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems should offer considered anonymity policies and evaluate the impact on review quality, reviewer accountability, and author safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of reviewer/researcher metrics and reputation systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics and reputation systems for reviewers and works (e.g., Publons, platform-level scores) are used as engagement incentives and recognition mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metric design should be critically evaluated for gaming risks, perverse incentives, fairness, and whether the metrics meaningfully reflect review quality rather than quantity.
